## Where we left off


- In Module 1 we fit models to a network we could **see**. 

   * Targets were based on those observed syringe sharing links: 

    ```r
    summary(fmh ~ edges + nodematch("Grade"))
    ```

- Often networks are less observable 
- Or network data are not directly available
- In such cases, available data are converted to ERGM-compatible target statistics for network parameters
- The network parameters are chosen to adequately describe the "generative" network structures of interest. 

::: notes
Recap in one breath: the intro had the whole adjacency matrix, so a "target" was
just a number we read off the network with `summary()`. Everything in this module
is about what happens when you *can't* do that.
:::

---

## The problem

Syringe-sharing among people who inject drugs is a **hidden network**.

- We cannot enumerate the population and map every tie (logistics, ethics)
- Sharing is stigmatized, partnerships are transient
- Hence, there is no observed graph to run `summary()` on

::: {.punch}
So where do the targets come from?
:::

::: notes
This is the motivating gap. Unlike a classroom friendship survey, we can't observe
the PWID sharing network. What we *do* have is survey and meta-analytic summaries:
how many partners people report, and who shares with whom by sex, age, and race.
:::

---

## The resolution

ERGMs can be fit to **summary statistics**, not just an observed network.

```r
ergm(net ~ terms, target.stats = <numbers>)
```

- We build an adjacency matrix from the data we have
- To do this, we turn survey statistics into a target vector 
- Checking ordering between the ERGM parameters and the target statistics is important, especially for parameters with multiple cells.  
- "From aggregate summaries to network parameters"...
- We produce a vector of summaries to specify in the ERGM.


::: notes
`target.stats` is the hinge of the workshop. Give ergm a set of numbers and it finds
the model whose expected statistics equal them. Our remaining work is translation:
survey summaries in, a target vector out. No fitting yet — that's Module 3.
:::

---

## Our Example

Network Characteristics:

  - n = 1,000 PWID with attributes: `sex`, `race.num`, `young`, `chicago`. 
  - The network is **directed**. 
  - That is, A naming B as a **syringe-sharing partner** is distinct from B naming A.

```r
library(network); library(ergm); library(dplyr); library(readr); library(here)

nodes   <- read_csv(here("data", "synthetic", "nodes.csv"))
targets <- readRDS(here("data", "synthetic", "targets.rds"))

net <- network.initialize(nrow(nodes), directed = TRUE)
for (col in names(nodes)) net %v% col <- nodes[[col]]
```


::: notes
The nodes come from the HepCEP synthetic population. Attributes are the ingredients
for the mixing terms. Directedness matters from here on and is the first real
departure from the intro. (Footnote, only if asked: these summaries are prepared at
our n = 1,000 working scale so ERGMs converge live in the room — the scaling isn't a
lesson, just data prep.)
:::

---

## Network "Features" of Interest

- Just as in the intro, we choose which network features (parameters) matter 

- This is driven by the *research question* 

- For syringe-sharing, transmission risk depends arguably on:
  - **How many partners people have** (degree distribution)
  - **Who shares with whom** — (i.e., homophily)

- Each feature becomes one or more terms in the ERGM specification

::: notes
Same move as the intro's null → assortative progression, just starting from survey
summaries instead of an observed graph. Degree distribution and mixing are the two
feature types this module builds targets for; Module 3 adds terms incrementally.
:::



## Degree Distribution {.smallish}

Modeling distributions of reported synringe-sharing partners

- The survey gives a **degree distribution**: how many people report 0, 1, 2, … partners. 

- Since this network is directed, we have in- and out-degrees as inputs.



| degree | # people (in) | # people (out) |
|:------:|:-------------:|:--------------:|
| 0 | 646 | 606 |
| 1 | 203 | 202 |
| 2 |  83 |  93 |
| 3 |  37 |  46 |
| … |  …  |  …  |
| ≥8 | ~1 | ~4 |


::: notes
This is our population of 1,000. Most people name few or no partners; a thin tail
names many. That skew is the structure we want to preserve — and it returns in
Module 3 as the `idegree`/`odegree` targets.
:::

---

## Turn a degree distribution into an edge count

- Every tie is one partner-slot for someone,
- **total ties = Σ (degree × # people at that degree)**, shown in the `num_n` column below
- Computed separately for in- and out-degree reports

```r
indeg  <- targets$indegree_data      # cols: in_degree, num_n
outdeg <- targets$outdegree_data     # num_n = num of people at in/out degree

inedges_target  <- sum(indeg$in_degree   * indeg$num_n)     # 630.8
outedges_target <- sum(outdeg$out_degree * outdeg$num_n)    # 791.5
```

::: notes
Pure bookkeeping — add up every partner-slot. No network required, just the
distribution. The two sums count the *same* edges from two directions.
:::

---

## Two estimates, one edge count → reconcile

- In-ties and out-ties count the same edges. Should agree. 
- They often don't in practice, because each is estimated separately. 
- Fixes possible based on available data. 
- Here, for simplicity, we take the mean.

```r
edges_target <- mean(c(inedges_target, outedges_target))     # 711
```

<!-- 
::: {.punch}
A target is a **count** — and the next step turns proportions *into* counts.
:::
 -->
::: notes
`711` is important to interpret. every mixing target is `edges_target × proportion`, so it
propagates through the whole vector. The in ≠ out gap is an honest preview —
summaries don't always reconcile, which is why simulation (Module 5), not the fit
object, is the real test of fit. (If asked about size/scale: the count and density
are size-dependent, but mean degree ≈ 0.71 and the mixing proportions are not — those
are what transfer across populations; Krivitsky, Handcock & Morris 2011.)
:::

---

## Homophily, one example: sex mixing

- The survey gives mixing as **proportions**.
- That is, the number of syringe sharing partners claimed by each sex (M/F).
- Claimed partners are istributed "within" the same group (i.e., M -> M, F->F) and "between" (i.e., M -> F,  F -> M) groups.   


```r
# shares of ties SENT by each sex
male_share <- 0.60; female_share <- 0.38

# within-group share of each sex's ties
male_within <- 0.55; female_within <- 0.72
```

ERGM specification

- Four numbers describe the whole sex-mixing pattern 
- The `ergm` function wants **counts** (not proportions).

::: notes
Same shape as `nodematch("sex")` in the intro, but unpacked: instead of one
within-group count, the survey gives us shares that split by direction and by
within/between group. That's the raw material — next slide turns it into targets.
:::

---

## From proportions to an ordered target

Multiply by `edges_target` to get counts, match `ergm`'s cell order, using
`summary()`'s output *names* as the source of truth:

```r
M_to_M <- edges_target * male_share   * male_within         # within-group
F_to_F <- edges_target * female_share * female_within       # within-group, reference
M_to_F <- edges_target * male_share   * (1 - male_within)
F_to_M <- edges_target * female_share * (1 - female_within)

summary(net ~ nodemix("sex", levels2 = -1))   # use this only for the cell NAMES / order
#>   mix.sex.F.M mix.sex.M.F mix.sex.M.M

sex_target <- c(F_to_M, M_to_F, M_to_M)        # targets, in that order:
#>   194.6       187.7       234.7             # fractional = proportions × edges_target (711.1)
```
Contains decimals, because targets are expected counts using means and proportions of the source data. 

::: notes
Why the target cells are fractional: they're proportions × edges_target (711.1) — expected
counts, not the integer tie counts `summary()` returns on a realized network. `summary()` here
is only for the names/order.

How ordering actually works: ergm sorts factor levels (here F before M) and enumerates
from→to combinations in that order, dropping the reference cell (`levels2 = -1`, the
first one). You never need to derive this by hand — `summary()` on the *unfitted*
formula returns the names before you fit anything, so the safest pattern is
`sex_target <- setNames(c(F_to_M, M_to_F, M_to_M), c("F_to_M","M_to_F","M_to_M"))[names(summary(net ~ nodemix("sex", levels2=-1)))]`
— match by name, not position, and a typo or mislabeled cell throws an error instead
of silently fitting the wrong model.
:::

---

## Rule of thumb

- Build a named vector
- Reorder it to match `summary()`'s names
- Specify the base term, e.g. `nodemix("sex", levels2 = -1)` 
- The `levels2` argument allows us to specify the base/ref. cell to avoid collinearity with `edges`. 
- A value of -1 drops the first term in the ordered vector. 


::: notes
This is the general recipe behind the worked example on the previous slide — it
scales to any `nodemix` term, not just sex.
:::

## Vector assembly

- Same conversion + ordering steps for `sex_target` scale to age and race mixing. 
- Each is its own `nodemix` term, concatenated in formula order:

```r
# age_target and race_target follow the sex_target example (see exercise)
target_vec <- c(edges_target, sex_target, age_target, race_target)
stopifnot(length(summary(f_mix)) == length(target_vec))   # count check, not order check
```

N.B.

- The count check catches a wrong **length**. 
- Only matching names catches a wrong **order**.

::: notes
We've fully worked edges and sex; age and race mixing follow the identical pattern
and are left as the exercise. `stopifnot` is a seatbelt, not a substitute for the
name-matching discipline from the last slide — a swapped pair of same-length cells
passes this check silently.
:::

---

## Handoff

- The `target_vec` vector is the output of this module 
- It contains Aggregate summaries converted to an ERGM-compatible vector. 
- Built off of partly observed data.

::: {.punch}
We have *parameters*, not yet a *model*. Module 3 fits an ERGM to `target_vec`.
:::

::: notes
This is the payoff of the module's title. Everything downstream — fitting (3),
diagnosing failure (4), simulation (5) — takes this vector as input.
:::
